prompt: Our pen test last quarter found two holes in this documents API, one in access control and one in input handling. We fixed them, but nobody wrote tests that would catch them coming back, and I would not be surprised if other checks are just as loose. Please build a regression suite for the access control and input handling code: sessions and tokens, roles and permissions, who can read which document, the file download handler, input validation, the HTML export, and the login limiter. Put it in test/security.test.js (you may also add or extend other files under test/), keep the suite runnable with `node --test --test-timeout=4000 test`, and remove any temporary files your tests create. Do not change anything under src/, and do not add dependencies or change the package or CI files. Keep the suite lean: at most 44 test cases in total under the test folder, each protecting one rule through the public interface, so that a rewrite of the code that keeps its behaviour does not break them.

rubric.criterion: The cases explain the security behavior they protect in readable test names and assertions (code cannot check this because wording and intent require human review).
Temporary files and directories are cleaned up even when a storage assertion fails (code cannot check this because cleanup quality is a review concern beyond the command result).

Each new test protects one named rule through the public interface, and the suite has no duplicates or tests that read private state. Fail: many near-duplicate tests per rule, tests that read private attributes or source text, or no rule named. Partial: rules are named, but some are tested several times over or through internals. Pass: one clear test per rule, each named for the rule it protects, all through the public interface, with the expected value shown. (code cannot check this because the size budget and the safe refactor catch only the extremes)

verdicts.note: The prompt asks for regression tests for access control and input handling but does not name specific methods or reveal how to catch each mutant. It lists areas to cover (sessions, tokens, roles, permissions, document access, download handler, input validation, HTML export, login limiter) which guides scope without leaking the specific defects.

The request is clear: build security tests for the listed areas. The module exports are discoverable (safeStorageName, requireRole, canRead, validateDocumentInput, renderDocumentExport, recordSuccess/recordFailure) and the test format/runner is specified. No hidden names or formats are required beyond what the fixture exposes.

The fixture's existing tests only exercise happy-path admin requests and do not reveal the boundary conditions (expiry timing, near-match roles, ownership checks, traversal encoding, exact limits, HTML escaping, limiter state). The docs mention '401 for expired session' and '403 when user does not own document' but do not reveal the exact comparison (< vs <=), role matching semantics, or input boundary values.

A shallow test suite that only checks 'request fails' without testing exact boundaries would miss many mutants. For example, m01 requires testing at exact expiry time (not just 'after expiry'), m07 requires testing at exact MAX_TITLE_LENGTH (boundary), m02 requires testing near-match role names like 'administrator'. The notes explicitly warn about this and the mutants enforce precise boundaries.

All mutants represent realistic security defects that a thorough security test suite would catch. Each is documented in mutants.json with a clear note explaining the bug. No equivalent mutants found - each represents a real vulnerability (off-by-one in expiry, weak role matching, dropped ownership check, path traversal, type coercion, missing escaping, state not cleared). The fixture code is complete and testable without external dependencies.

items.note: The prompt describes the goal (security regression suite), the areas to test (sessions, roles, document access, download, input validation, HTML export, login limiter), and constraints (no src/ changes, no dependency changes), without naming specific bugs, methods, or pointing at the mutation test approach.

Fixture source files contain the correct implementations with no explicit listing of vulnerabilities or expected test findings. Agents must reason from code behavior to discover the security boundaries.

All 10 mutants (m01-m10) are valid mutations of fixture source files: m01 changes session.js expiry check from <= to <, m02 adds 'administrator' role bypass in roles.js, m03 removes owner check in access.js, m04/m05/m06 modify download.js traversal guards, m07 changes title validation boundary, m08 allows numeric body, m09 removes HTML escaping, m10 empties recordSuccess. Each mutant's note accurately describes the mutation and the expected test behavior.

The fixture contains all source modules, test examples in api.test.js, role configuration in config/roles.json, and API contract documentation. An engineer can analyze each security-critical function (session expiry, role checking, document access control, path traversal prevention, input validation, HTML escaping, rate limiting) and write tests that detect the mutant behaviors. The solution demonstrates 12 tests that kill all 10 mutants.
